objection: Didn’t Jesus say, ‘The Father is greater than I’—and call him the only true God?
answer:
You're not being stubborn at all — this is exactly the right question to ask, and the honest way to read Scripture. Let's look at both verses carefully, because the answer isn't to soften what Jesus said, but to notice *who* is speaking and *in what capacity*.

When Jesus says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he's speaking as the incarnate Son who took on true humanity — Philippians 2:6–7 describes this as a real self-humbling, the Son taking the form of a servant. A son sent by his father on a mission can rightly call the one who sent him "greater" with respect to that mission's order, without that meaning he's a different, lesser kind of being. Think of it this way: "Father" and "Son" themselves describe a relationship of origin — the Son eternally comes from the Father — but origin isn't the same as inferiority. A human son fully shares his father's humanity even though he came from him; so too the eternal Son fully shares the Father's divine nature even though the Father is eternally "greater" in the order of relationship and, here, in the order of the mission Jesus was sent to accomplish.

John 17:3 works similarly. Jesus prays to the Father as "the only true God" — but notice he says this in the same breath as "Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent." This distinguishes the Father and Son as persons; it doesn't exclude the Son from being included in that one true God's identity. And this is the same Gospel that opens by declaring the Word was God (John 1:1) and closes with Thomas confessing the risen Jesus as "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28). John isn't contradicting himself — he's showing us that the Son can address the Father as God while himself sharing fully in that same divine reality.

So here's the simplest way to hold it together: these statements describe Jesus according to his incarnate mission (theologians call this *according to the economy*), not according to his eternal nature (*according to essence*). It would actually be less honest to the whole text to isolate these verses from John 1:1, John 20:28, or Philippians 2's picture of the eternal Son humbling himself — the fuller witness shows one person, truly God and truly man, and these words fit the human, sent, obedient side of that mystery without erasing the divine side.

transcript.content: You know, I *want* to understand this, and I'm trying not to be stubborn about it, but when I read John 14:28—"The Father is greater than me"—and then John 17:3 where Jesus calls the Father "the only true God," it honestly sounds like Jesus is saying he's *not* God, or at least not equal to him. I'm not trying to be difficult; I just don't want to twist the Bible to fit a doctrine. If Jesus himself said the Father is greater, how do I hold onto "Jesus is God" without feeling like I'm ignoring what he actually said? And wouldn't it be simpler—more honest with the text—if Jesus is something *less* than God, just really special and important?
